chapter: Los Angeles with Mutt Carey and the taxi dances
title: Playing on camera in silent films like The Road to Ruin
summary: Joe and Mutt's band appeared in a barn-dance scene in his first movie, playing live for atmosphere because the union required musicians.

bands.name: Satchel McVea and His Howdy Band

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Well, in chronological order, like you say, we'll talk about whatever happened around Los Angeles... Like I said, they had a lot of taxi dances, and once in a while, we played in the studios. Now, people said, 'What are you guys doing playing in the studios with silent movies' -- this is the time of the silents. But they had them just for atmosphere.
You mean playing in the pit.

Well, just playing on the side in the studio. For instance, the first movie I ever made was called A Road To Ruin, with Sally Allis(?) and I'm trying to think of the other actor's name. And I worked in a thing with Gary Cooper called The Legend Of The Condemned.
I've seen a movie from '29, '30 or someplace where there's no sound, but there's a picture of you and Mutt...
Yeah. It's a barn dance scene.
Yeah. You've got some straw hats on.
Darensbourg - 157
Straw hats and overalls.
What movie was that?
That was The Road To Ruin.
That was the first one.
That was the first one I ever worked in. And we got that... Certainly you know Jack McVea.
Sure.

He wrote "Open The Door, Richard." Well, his Dad was an old-time banjo player who played a five-string banjo, that had a good connection with the studios. His name was... He called any group he got together Satchel McVea and His Howdy Band. I carried his card around for years, I thought it was such an unusual name.

When you made this particular movie, for instance... Because I know what that's about, and I've seen the thing. I've only seen the little bit with you guys in it. But you're only on there for a minute-and-a-half even if that...
Yes, it's a very short scene.
So you'd actually been playing the music, but it wouldn't be recorded. Nobody would be recording it.
That's right. Oh yeah, we played something.
Darensbourg - 158
What was the point... Why didn't they just hire extras to look like they were playing?
The union wouldn't let them do it.
Oh, the union. Okay.

Right now for atmosphere music, they could do the same thing. 90 percent of these music scenes you see now is recorded before by studio musicians. But you hire those atmosphere musicians for a lot of reasons. Because if you're filming something and you make some mistakes or cut a hog, and (?)they can't take it(?), it's going to cost them that much more money. So that music is dubbed in there...
But in this particular film, you actually were playing the music as you...
Oh, we played. And you could play whatever you wanted to play.
It's a shame nobody ever recorded that.
But it wasn't recorded.
That's a shame.
You see?
Yeah.
